Positioning by Exam: Projections, Topographical Landmarks, and Reading the Requisition

Unit 1: Anatomy, Positioning, and Medical Language. Lesson 4 of 60 in CRES Academy.

Positioning is a radiographer's skill, but every one of its requirements is a demand on your equipment: a distance that must be repeatable, a detent that must land, a lamp that must show the field, a marker that must appear on the image.

Projections, named for where the beam goes

  • AP: the beam enters the front and exits the back, with the patient facing the tube. PA: it enters the back and exits the front, with the patient facing the receptor, which puts the anatomy closer to the detector and magnifies less.
  • Lateral: the beam crosses side to side, and the named side is the one against the receptor.
  • Oblique: the body is rotated between frontal and lateral while the tube and receptor stay square. RAO puts the right front against the receptor, LAO the left front, RPO the right back, LPO the left back.
  • Axial runs along the long axis of a part; tangential skims a surface to throw other anatomy clear; decubitus is lying down with a horizontal beam.

Distances and the central ray

The source-to-image receptor distance is standardized so one technique repeats: about 100 cm for routine work, 180 cm for chest, and about 90 cm on some special units. The object-to-image receptor distance is the gap between the anatomy and the detector, and keeping it short is what keeps the image sharp. The central ray is the center of the beam, aimed at the center of the part and the center of the detector. Collimate to the part, and put a left or right marker in the field, not on the anatomy.

Topographic lines and landmarks

Orbitomeatal line       outer corner of the eye to the ear canal
Infraorbitomeatal line  just below the eye to the ear canal
Glabellomeatal line     the glabella between the eyebrows to the ear canal
Acanthiomeatal line     the acanthion where nose meets upper lip to the ear canal
T1                      about 2 inches above the sternal notch
T2 to T3                the sternal notch; T4 to T5 the sternal angle
T6 to T7                the lower end of the scapula; T10 the xiphoid tip

Those points are the body's surface topography, the bony landmarks a radiographer finds by feel, and spinal topography is the same idea along the vertebral column, which is how a chart says where to center. The skull lines are how a manual tells you to set tube and table angles, so an angle readout that is out by a few degrees becomes a positioning complaint.

The requisition and the identifying markers

A requisition carries the patient identifiers, the exam requested, the side, the relevant history, and pregnancy status. Every image must carry the patient's full name, a unique identifier, date of birth, the date it was made, anatomic markers for right and left, the patient's orientation, any time interval used, whether a chest was made on inspiration or expiration, and sequence markers when it belongs to a series. When a console loses that overlay after a software change, you have a compliance problem, not a cosmetic one.

Positional terminology as the equipment sees it

The same anatomy needs a different setup in every modality: a radiographic room sets table angle, tube angle, detector height, and distance; computed tomography sets patient orientation, laser alignment, and table increment; ultrasound needs only access and gel. Anatomy, technique, and position are one package, which is why a positioning complaint is checked as geometry: distance indicator, angle readout, detents, lamp, and collimation.

Exam tip: AP enters the front, PA enters the back, and the named oblique or lateral side is the one closest to the receptor. Routine distance about 100 cm, chest 180 cm. Learn the four skull lines and the thoracic landmarks, and know that markers and identifiers on the image are required, not optional.
Remember
AP, PA, lateral, the obliques RAO, LAO, RPO, and LPO, plus axial, tangential, and decubitus name where the beam goes; distance is about 100 cm routine and 180 cm for chest with the object-to-image distance kept short; the orbitomeatal, infraorbitomeatal, glabellomeatal, and acanthiomeatal lines and the T1 to T10 landmarks set the angles; and every image must carry name, identifier, date of birth, date, anatomic markers, orientation, time interval, inspiration or expiration, and sequence.
Deeper explanation

Positioning by Exam: Projections, Topographical Landmarks, and Reading the Requisition, explained slowly

Projections are named for the beam, positions for the patient

Getting this straight settles half the vocabulary. A projection names the path of the central ray through the body: anteroposterior enters the front and leaves the back, posteroanterior the reverse. A position names how the patient is placed: supine, prone, erect, recumbent, oblique, decubitus. The oblique names combine them, and the letter order tells you everything: the first letter is the side, the second whether the front or back of that side faces the receptor.

RAO   right anterior oblique    right front against the receptor
LAO   left anterior oblique     left front against the receptor
RPO   right posterior oblique   right back against the receptor
LPO   left posterior oblique    left back against the receptor

Posterior obliques are what you get from a patient who cannot be turned off their back, which is why trauma and bedside work are full of them. Through all of it the tube and receptor stay square to each other and the patient rotates, so what the equipment must provide is rotation detents, a reliable centering indicator, and an angle readout you can trust.

The geometry numbers

Quantity                            Standard value          Why it matters
Source-to-image distance (SID)      about 100 cm routine    repeatability; the figure the chart assumes
                                    180 cm chest            less magnification of the heart
                                    about 90 cm on some     special-purpose units
Object-to-image distance (OID)      kept as short as        magnification and blur both grow with it
                                    possible
Magnification factor (MF)           SID / SOD               about 1.1 at 100 cm, 1.05 at 180 cm
Light field to radiation field      within 2 percent of     2 cm at a 100 cm distance
                                    the SID

Those last two lines are where positioning becomes your problem: the radiographer centers to a lamp, so if the lamp and the beam disagree, every image is mispositioned no matter how good the technique.

The skull lines and the thoracic landmarks

Orbitomeatal line        outer canthus of the eye to the ear canal
Infraorbitomeatal line   just below the eye to the ear canal
Glabellomeatal line      the glabella between the eyebrows to the ear canal
Acanthiomeatal line      the acanthion, where nose meets upper lip, to the ear canal
T1                       about 2 inches above the sternal notch
T2 to T3                 the sternal notch at the jugular
T4 to T5                 the sternal angle
T6 to T7                 the lower end of the scapula
T10                      the xiphoid tip

Skull procedures are written as a tube angle relative to one of those lines, so an angle indicator reading a few degrees off, or a detent that no longer lands at zero, becomes a stream of repeated skull images.

The requisition, and what must be on the image

A requisition carries the patient identifiers, the examination requested, which side, relevant history, and pregnancy status. The image itself must carry: the patient's full name; one unique identifier, normally the medical record number; the date of birth; the acquisition date, without which no later study can be compared against this one; anatomic markers for right and left, placed with a radiopaque marker; the patient's orientation; the time interval, where one was used; whether a chest was made on inspiration or expiration, and sequence markers if it belongs to a series. That list is a compliance list, not a preference. After a console software change or a worklist reconfiguration, check that the overlay still carries every field, because an image that cannot be identified is an image that cannot be used.

One anatomy, four setups

The same part needs a different arrangement in every modality, which is the practical meaning of the relationship between anatomy, technique, and positioning.

Radiography      table angle, tube angle, detector height, distance, collimation, markers
Fluoroscopy      table tilt and detents, spot image geometry, the spacer that sets minimum distance
Computed tomog.  patient orientation, laser alignment, table increment and travel accuracy
Ultrasound       access and gel only; the probe is the geometry

So when a positioning complaint arrives, you check geometry in this order: distance indicator, collimator lamp and light field accuracy, angle readouts, detents and locks, detector height, and the marker and overlay fields. Every one of those is measurable, and that is what separates your part of the complaint from the radiographer's.

What to memorize

  • AP enters the front, PA enters the back; the named oblique or lateral side is nearest the receptor.
  • About 100 cm routine, 180 cm chest; keep the object-to-image distance short; the light field must match the beam within 2 percent of the distance.
  • Four skull lines: orbitomeatal, infraorbitomeatal, glabellomeatal, acanthiomeatal.
  • Landmarks T1 about 2 inches above the sternal notch, T2 to T3 the notch, T4 to T5 the sternal angle, T6 to T7 the scapula's lower end, T10 the xiphoid.
  • The nine image identifiers, and that they are required.
